name: Olga Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy garden and pet supplies for Greenpaw Distribution: compost, bird feed, dog chews, plant pots, the lot. We supply garden centres and pet shops, and everything is seasonal. I start with a coffee and my AI assistant, which pulls last week's sales into a summary so I can see what's moving. Then I do supplier calls, then planning spring orders, which I start in November.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers game: if I order four hundred bags of bird seed and the winter's mild, I've got a problem. I enjoy using clever tools to reduce the guessing. What wears me out is when the weather or a shipping delay wrecks a plan I've spent weeks on. My husband Dan drives a city bus, and we've got Maya, eleven, and Joe, eight. The mortgage and school costs eat everything, and we've almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, we've got what we've got. At work I'd tell the team that the tools we already have are good if you set them up well. Online I'd say the world's calmer than the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I wouldn't mind. I've already built a couple of small automations that save me hours, and I'd keep improving those. It does mean my edge stays about the same, and I like having an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building. I'd tidy up my demand-forecast sheet, share the template with the others, and maybe get a small bonus for it. I'd keep checking every figure the tools give me, because they do get things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit flat, because I like change, but I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about how you use AI day to day, and what would change if it stopped improving.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. We've got maybe two weeks of savings, and Dan's shift pay swings. When my daughter needed glasses and my son needed a dentist in the same month, we pushed the credit card. That's what's pressing, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's already pressing on you at home or at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm's margins, too. Garden centres are squeezed, and they squeeze us. A bad spring is the thing I actually lose sleep over.

say: I'd tell the team the tools we have are **good** if you set them up well.
Online I'd say the world is calmer than the headlines.
think: I wouldn't mind this; I'd keep improving my own **automations** and keep my edge.
Our real pressure is **money**, with two weeks of savings.
do: Tidy my **forecast sheet**, share the template and ask for a small bonus.
Keep checking every number the tools give me.
Set aside money before the next family **bill** lands.
feel: **Flat** but not worried; I like change, so a quiet world is a little dull.
S0.quote: When my daughter needed glasses and my son needed a dentist in the same month, we pushed the credit card.
fieldNote: Olga's mood is **uneasy** because her money is thin, even though AI barely matters here.
She already automates her own work and wants credit for it.
She is most afraid of a bad spring, not of technology.

steps.text: Tidy the demand-forecast sheet and share it with the team
Keep checking every number the AI tools give me
Ask for a bonus for the hours my sheet saves
Put fifty a week into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let's put me in charge of the pilots, because I'm already doing it. Online I'd say it's going to help people who adapt and hurt people who can't, so we have to look after both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm fine for a few years, because I'm the one the firm will ask to run the tools. But Greenpaw's buying team of seven turns into three or four, and I know the others. I'd call myself one of the winners, and strangely I still don't feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over forecasting for the whole range and automate the weekly reorders. I'd ask for a team-lead title with real money. I'd also write a guide for the others so they can use the tools, because I'd rather lose colleagues slowly than overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, and a bit sad. I like my work, and it's changing under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on the list of jobs AI takes over. What would be left of your role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps owners and fast adopters, and hurts the ones who only enter orders. It hurts the garden centres too, who may get squeezed by bigger platforms. People who stick to one skill are the most at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who does this help most, and who does it hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a pay rise before the cuts, not after. If the firm is about to save money on the team, the person running the tools should see some of it. And I'd save the whole raise.

say: I'd say put me in charge of the **pilots**, since I'm already doing it.
I'd say it helps people who adapt and hurts those who can't, so we must look after **both**.
think: I'm fine for a few years because I'm the one the firm asks to run the tools.
A buying team of seven becomes **three or four**, and I still don't feel safe.
do: Take over **forecasting** for the whole range and automate the weekly reorders.
Ask for a team-lead title with **real money** before cuts.
Write a guide so colleagues can use the tools.
feel: **Excited**, mostly, and a bit sad that my work is changing under me.
S1.quote: I'd call myself one of the winners, and strangely I still don't feel safe.
fieldNote: Olga expects to be a **winner** inside the firm yet still feels exposed.
She asks for the raise before cuts and wants to be paid for running the tools.
Writing a guide for colleagues shows she cares about the slower ones.

steps.text: Take over forecasting for the whole range using AI tools
Write a plain guide to the tools for colleagues
Ask for a team-lead title and raise before any cuts
Save the whole raise for a six-month cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to move faster than any plan on the table. Online I'd be arguing the rules have to catch up with what we're about to see, and I'd be asking who owns the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hits me hard. If AI does all thinking work better than me for cheaper, my edge is gone. Dan's job, driving a bus, will last until about 2031, which buys us some time, but not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month: I'd talk to the owners about moving into running the AI systems, or into something that involves people, like supplier relations. I'd start a side venture, maybe selling forecasting setups to small garden centres. And we'd cut the budget to the minimum and sit down with Dan to plan a worst-case year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. It's like waiting for a result. I'd feel energy, because I like solving things, and I'd be worried sick at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Within two years. How does the job look to you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also talk to a financial adviser, or at least a free service, about how to handle the mortgage. With two weeks of savings, I can't gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan's bus job is hands-on, so it holds for the first three years after the card, and that's what I'd lean on. I'd want us to move to one income as the plan B, with me taking part-time bits.

say: I'd say we need to move faster than any plan on the table.
Online I'd ask **who owns** the machines and push for rules.
think: If AI does all thinking work better and cheaper, my **edge** is gone.
Dan's bus job lasts until about 2031, which buys some time, but not enough.
do: Ask the owners to move me into **running the AI systems** or supplier relations.
Start a side venture selling **forecasting setups** to small garden centres.
Plan a worst-case year with Dan and cut the budget.
feel: **Anxious** and wired; energised by solving things, worried sick at night.
S2.quote: If AI does all thinking work better than me for cheaper, my edge is gone.
fieldNote: Olga reacts by **building**: a side venture and a new role.
Dan's hands-on job is her cushion for the first three years.
She cannot gamble, with two weeks of savings.

steps.text: Ask the owners for a role running the AI buying systems
Sell forecasting setups to small garden centres on the side
Cut the household budget to the minimum
Get free mortgage advice from a debt charity

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if people start now. At work I'd push for a pay-while-you-train scheme. Online I'd probably share useful guides on learning the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the buying role as it exists is gone by 2031, but I'm the type to be one step ahead. My worry is that every similar person is doing the same, so the field gets crowded. I'd need something that fits me, not just the crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: start the side business properly, with three paying customers. Take a data-and-operations certificate. Save three hundred a month, because I'd like three months' expenses before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but driven. The time gives me something to do, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives some room. What do you do now that you wouldn't do in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn how things work, not just how to use them. I'd show them what I do with the tools and explain that work changes. I wouldn't tell them what job to aim for, because I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell the kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I like about five years is I can test the side venture while Dan keeps his job. If it fails, we've lost a little. If it works, we've got a second income.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if people start now.
I'd push for a pay-while-you-train scheme at work.
think: The buying role as it exists is gone by **2031**, but I'm the type to be a step ahead.
My worry is that everyone similar does the same and the field gets crowded.
do: Start the side business properly and win **three paying customers**.
Save three hundred a month towards **three months** of expenses.
feel: **Anxious** but driven; the time gives me something to do.
S3.quote: I'd tell my kids to learn how things work, not just how to use them.
fieldNote: Olga uses time to **test** a side income while her husband's job is secure.
She sees crowding as a risk for adaptable people too.
She is honest that she can't tell her children what job to aim for.

steps.text: Win three paying customers for the forecasting side business
Take a data-and-operations certificate on weekday evenings
Save three hundred a month towards three months of expenses
Show Maya and Joe how I use AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and it'd be silly not to use it. At work I'd be building the next version of what we do. Online I'd talk about the practical side, like the best courses for different jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm comfortable. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be at university, and I'd have a few extra income lines. I'd be ready, which I can't say for most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a steady job and build gradually. I'd do a part-time master's in operations or data, grow the side business and save for the kids' education. Every year I'd drop one thing from my routine that a tool could do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some excitement. It feels like a project with a deadline, and I like those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What changes in the way you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments should pay for retraining and a basic income floor, firms should give notice and fair exits, and people should put in the effort. I'd rather say that than blame one group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be responsible for helping people through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing my own team to learn too. It's easier to be adaptive when you aren't doing it alone.

say: I'd say ten years is generous and it would be silly not to **use it**.
Online I'd share the best courses for different jobs.
think: I'm comfortable: by 2036 the kids are at university and I'd have **extra income lines**.
I'd be ready, which I can't say for most people.
do: Keep a steady job and do a part-time **master's** in operations or data.
Grow the side business and save for the kids' **education**.
Drop one task each year that a tool does better.
feel: **Calm**, with some excitement, like a project with a deadline.
S4.quote: Governments should pay for retraining and a basic income floor, firms should give notice and fair exits, and people should put in the effort.
fieldNote: With a decade, Olga's mood is only **uneasy**, because of thin savings today.
She spreads blame across governments, firms and people.

steps.text: Do a part-time master's in operations or data
Grow the side business to a second steady income
Save for Maya's and Joe's university costs
Hand one routine task a year to a tool

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even though I'd move fast, we've got two weeks of savings and I'd have no time to build a second income. What would help is a government income floor, retraining that pays while you do it, and employers giving fair notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say adaptable people carry a quiet pressure too. People assume adaptable people will be fine because we move quickly, but I still have a mortgage and two kids to cover while I'm doing it.

headlineQuote: People assume adaptable people will be fine because we move quickly, but I still have a mortgage and two kids to cover while I'm doing it.
portrait: Olga Evans, 43, is a senior **buyer** of garden and pet supplies, with a bus-driver husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She's centrist and **adaptive**: she uses AI daily, builds her own forecasting tools and wants credit for them.
Her money is thin, about two weeks saved, so she stays uneasy even when AI plateaus.
In faster scenarios she expects the buying role to shrink and builds a **side business** and a new role.
She leans on Dan's hands-on bus job for the first few years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because she can't build a second income in time with so little savings.
whatWouldHelp: A government **income floor**, paid retraining and fair notice from employers.
